question.leadin: Answer the following about the landmark interstate commerce case Gibbons v. Ogden.
question.text: This American entrepreneur, nicknamed "Commodore," worked as a steamboat captain and business manager for Gibbons, and combatted other steamboat monopolies before building a railroad empire.
question.clue: During the California Gold Rush, this person created the Accessory Transit Company to bring passengers from the East Coast to San Francisco via Nicaragua.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about conflicts over speech at educational institutions.
swap.text: In 1943, the Supreme Court held that students could not be forced to recite this statement, which is often said daily in schools and ends with the words "with liberty and justice for all".
swap.clue: In 1943, Jehovah's Witnesses argued that engaging in this practice constituted veneration in the landmark case West Virginia vs. Barnette.

question.text: During his second term, Cleveland sent in troops to put down this 1894 strike based on his constitutional responsibility to have mail delivered. This railroad strike was led by Eugene V. Debs.
question.clue: Governor John Atgeld was opposed to the federal response to this event, which occurred after the disruption of the mail service.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about presidential assassinations.
swap.text: This immigrant, a disciple of the anarchist Emma Goldman, traveled to Buffalo and shot William McKinley in a reception line at the 1901 Pan-American Exposition.
swap.clue: Note to Moderator: Be generous on pronunciation. While Robert Todd Lincoln was outside the Temple of Music at the 1901 Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, New York, this anarchist shot William McKinley.

question.text: Before becoming mayor, La Guardia joined Moses in the Fusion Party to challenge this New York political machine once led by Boss Tweed.
question.clue: To gain power as a sachem of this society, "Honest" John Kelly aided Samuel Tilden in fighting this organization's corruption.

swap.text: After Farragut captured New Orleans, this general led the city's occupation, instituting a quarantine to curb the spread of yellow fever. He had earlier refused to return fugitive slaves to the Confederacy as "contraband of war."
swap.clue: While commanding the garrison at Fort Monroe, this man claimed the right of "contraband of war" while refusing to return fugitive slaves.

question.leadin: This man had a spat with Rutherford B. Hayes over patronage at a Customs House.
question.text: Name this leader of the Stalwarts, who opposed the Half-Breed's calls for Civil Service reform. He was the mentor of Chester Arthur.
question.clue: To protest William H. Robertson's appointment as Port Collector, this man resigned from the Senate with his longtime ally Thomas C. Platt.

swap.text: Guiteau assassinated this president, who served only seven months in office. This man's Secretary of State was James Blaine, and he was succeeded by Chester A. Arthur.
swap.clue: This man defeated Winfield Scott Hancock to become president, and the Pendleton Civil Service Act was passed after his death.

question.leadin: Identify the following about undercover reporting during the Gilded Age.
question.text: This woman asked, "Could I pass a week in the insane ward at Blackwell's Island? I said I could and I would. And I did" in the intro to her undercover report for the New York World. She also wrote Around the World in Seventy-Two Days.
question.answerHtml: Nellie Bly [or Elizabeth Cochrane Seaman; or Elizabeth Jane Cochran]
question.clue: This person declared that "Mexico is a Republic in name only. It is the worst monarchy existence" in a nonfiction book based on her time living six months under the reign of Porfirio Diaz.

swap.leadin: Answer some questions about some superficially related organizations from American history.
swap.text: One of the bigger names to join the Anti-Imperialist League was this Scottish-born industrialist, whose Pittsburgh-based steel company was bought out by J. P. Morgan for $480 million.
swap.clue: This man donated almost $50 million to American public library systems in accordance with the ideas he outlined in his "Gospel of Wealth."

question.leadin: Name these things about American moral crusaders.
question.text: Frances Willard was a key leader and the eventual president of this feminist organization, which lobbied for universal suffrage and prison reform, in addition to the defining item of its agenda, prohibition.
question.clue: This group, which used the slogan "For God and Home and Every Land" and was led by Annie Wittenmyer, adopted a Xenophon quote to argue for "total abstinence from everything harmful."

swap.leadin: The 1928 Meriam Report's criticism of this law led to its repeal with the Wheeler-Howard Act in 1934.
swap.text: Name this 1887 law that forced Native American tribes with traditional usage of communal land to switch to individual ownership of private property. Through this act, the US government stole 100 million acres of tribal land.
swap.answerHtml: Dawes Act [or Dawes Severalty Act of 1887; or General Allotment Act]
swap.clue: This law attempted to eliminate the Native American "communal" way of living by dividing tribal land into allotments of 160 acres for families and 80 acres for individuals.

question.text: One of the most important events of the "Erie War" was when Gould gained the support of this Tammany Hall figure by making him a member of the board of the Erie Railroad.
question.clue: In an 1871 cover of Harper's Weekly, Thomas Nast used the phrase "To the victors belong the spoils" to depict a beat-up version of this then "boss" of Tammany Hall.

swap.text: This founder of the New-York Tribune, a radical promoter of socialism and temperance, was the Liberal Republican Party's presidential nominee in the 1872 election.
swap.clue: He died a broken man, having lost his most prized business venture to Whitelaw Reid.

question.leadin: Answer the following about traditional and revivalist religions among Native Americans.
question.text: Joseph Epes Brown collected descriptions of seven Oglala religious rites from this holy man. More famously, John Neihardt collected stories, ritual descriptions, and history of the Oglala into a work wherein this man "Speaks".

swap.leadin: Bombs, Bullets, and Business as Usual subtitled a 2011 documentary by Richard Weller about a particularly detonation-prone one of these places.
swap.text: A man using the pseudonym "Roy Walsh" placed a device made from an egg timer and a VCR in a bathroom in one of these places, but the person he intended to assassinate happened to be up late writing a speech.
swap.clue: Charles Evans Hughes determined that some of these places in Washington state were subject to a minimum wage law in a 1937 case whose plaintiff was Elsie Parrish, and which ended the "Lochner Era".

question.text: This institution in Upstate New York was founded by Lewis Miller and John Heyl Vincent as a teaching camp for Sunday school teachers. It included Palestine Park, a scale model of the Holy Land.
question.clue: This institution that names a late 19th-century adult education movement whose lecturers and entertainers, including Russell Conwell, reached 35 million people on its "circuit."

swap.leadin: This man broke with William McKinley over what he regarded as McKinley's expansionist policies with respect to Cuba and Hawaii.
swap.text: Identify this politician from Maine, whose major political innovation as House Speaker was to institute his namesake rules which ensured that the House would be controlled by the majority party.
swap.clue: This Republican, occasionally nicknamed "Czar," became Speaker following a fight with William McKinley. He had earlier served on the Potter Commission to investigate the Election of 1876.

question.leadin: The only time this political party nominated a candidate who won the presidency was in 1928 when it also nominated the Republican ticket of Hoover and Curtis. FTPE.
question.text: Name this party that nominated people such as Earl Dodge, John Bidwell and James Black, and supported the passage of the Volstead Act.
question.clue: They allowed Grover Cleveland to carry New York with the strong 1884 showing of John St. John, but their best results came in the next two presidential elections, in which Clinton Fisk and John Bidwell polled over 200,000 votes.

swap.text: Identifying "democratic" and "legislative" types of government, this speech given in Chicago at the DNC of 1896 ends with the speaker claiming "you shall not crucify mankind" on the title object.
